name: Rosa Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the first term of a law degree at Harlow University, and I cycle in because the bus is too dear. Mornings are lectures, afternoons are the library or a tutorial, and I work behind the counter at Singh's Pharmacy three evenings and every other Saturday. I'm the first in my family to do this, so my head is always half in the textbook and half on the rota.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hardest right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my grandmother, Nani, in the flat above a laundrette. My dad left when I was little and my mum works nights cleaning offices, so nobody can pay for me. I got a top grade and a scholarship that covers some of the fees, and loans cover the rest. I use an AI chatbot now and then to untangle cases I don't understand, but I always check the real judgment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one's called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and that it's overhyped, like most tech. At the pharmacy they bought a stock-ordering system, and it just made more mistakes for the staff to fix. I'd tell friends to keep studying and not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if nothing changes, I'm not relaxed. The loans are real, Nani's rent is going up, and my hours at the pharmacy aren't guaranteed. Law firms are also hiring fewer trainees already, so I can't count on a job just because I got good grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep my grades up and try for a pro bono society placement in my second year. I'd also put a few pounds a month in a savings pot, even a small one, because I have nothing. And I'd keep using the chatbot as a study helper, not a shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, but fine. I'm used to not having much slack. I'd feel more worried about the rent than about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money is tight. What gives first if your pharmacy hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the savings and my bus fare, then I'd ask Mr Singh for more evenings. If that failed I'd look for an extra tutoring job. I would never drop a lecture, because the scholarship needs my marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a plateau change how you think about law as a career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Law is still about talking to real people and convincing them. But the competition for trainee places is so hard that having top marks isn't enough, and I'd need work experience too.

say: I'd tell friends AI is **overhyped**, and to keep studying rather than panic.
At the pharmacy the new ordering system made **more mistakes** for staff to fix.
think: Even if nothing changes, **loans** and Nani's rising rent keep me worried.
Law firms already hire **fewer trainees**, so good grades alone won't be enough.
do: Keep working at the **pharmacy** and keep my grades up for the scholarship.
Try for a **pro bono** placement in my second year.
Put a few pounds a month in a **savings pot**.
feel: A bit **tense**, but used to having no slack. I worry more about rent than robots.
S0.quote: I'd feel more worried about the rent than about robots.
fieldNote: Her anxiety here is **money and trainee places**, not AI.
Uses the chatbot as a study aid but checks the source, a sign of steady habits.
Already thinking about a pro bono placement to build her record.

steps.text: Keep the three evening shifts at Singh's Pharmacy
Put aside ten pounds a month in a savings pot
Ask the law school about hardship funding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one's called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to regulate and protect people. Firms shouldn't be able to swap staff for software and keep all the savings. I'd say it online and at the law society, because a lot of us are listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Law is thinking work, so I think it's hit hard. Research, checking contracts and drafting are what trainees do, and they're what the tools do well. That means fewer places, and I'm no longer sure that top marks will protect me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at using the tools now, because I'd rather lead than be replaced. I'd join the law society's technology group and aim for roles involving people, such as housing or immigration, where clients need a real person. I'd keep the pharmacy job because the money is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but also a bit fired up. It would be scary, but I'd rather be in a profession that's changing than one that's already gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of a law student's work do you expect the tools to take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Document review, checking and first drafts. That's the junior work. My Nani's rent dispute with the landlord took a human who listened, so I'd go where that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fund for retraining that pays a wage, and rules that say humans must stay in charge of legal decisions. I'd want the cost of change to fall on the firms that profit, not on students like me.

say: I'd say it's the moment to **regulate** and protect people, not let firms keep all the savings.
I'd say it online and at the **law society**.
think: Research, contract checking and drafting are junior **law work**, and the tools do them well.
I'm no longer sure **top marks** will protect me.
do: Learn the **AI tools** now so I can lead rather than be replaced.
Aim for **housing or immigration** work, where clients need a real person.
feel: **Nervous** but fired up: I'd rather be in a field that's changing than one already gone.
S1.quote: I'd get better at using the tools now, because I'd rather lead than be replaced.
fieldNote: She turns worry into **action**, taking on the tools to stay ahead.
Her view comes from seeing her grandmother's rent dispute, so a real person matters to her.
Expects fewer trainee places but not none.

steps.text: Join the law society's technology group
Use an AI tool for case summaries and check them against the judgments
Write to my MP about rules for firms replacing staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one's called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and that the government should call people together now. Two years isn't enough for law schools or families to change anything. I'd probably be the one at the student meeting asking for emergency funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate straight into the middle of it. If AI can do all the thinking work by then, a law degree might not lead to anything, and I'd have debt I can't pay. I'd feel I'd chosen the wrong thing, even though I worked so hard for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the pharmacy job and ask for more hours. It's hands-on work with real customers, so it's safe for longer. I'd talk to a careers adviser about switching to something like pharmacy technician training, and I'd stop adding loan for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'd keep thinking about Nani and Mum, and how they can't help me. I'd cry once and then make a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, how would you change what you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at pharmacy, healthcare or social care because people still want a person there. I wouldn't give up on law completely, but I'd treat it as a maybe and not the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum and Nani?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth and that I've got a list. Mum would say don't give up, and Nani would say come home and eat. They can't fix it, but they make me feel less alone.

say: I'd say **two years** is too fast and families should be called together now.
I'd go to the student meeting and ask for **emergency funding**.
think: A law degree might lead **nowhere** if the thinking work is gone, and I'd owe debt.
I'd feel I chose the **wrong thing** after working so hard.
do: Keep the pharmacy job and ask for **more hours**.
See a careers adviser about **pharmacy technician** training.
Stop adding to my **loan** until I know what's real.
feel: **Scared**: I'd cry once, and then make a list.
S2.quote: I'd cry once and then make a list.
fieldNote: The **pharmacy job** becomes her safe ground because it is hands-on.
She keeps law as a possibility and does not drop it in panic.
Family cannot help financially, but they give her comfort.

steps.text: Ask Mr Singh for more evening hours at the pharmacy
Book a careers adviser for pharmacy technician training
Apply for a part-time healthcare assistant role
Tell Mum and Nani the plan and ask the hardship fund for help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one's called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us do something properly. We could write the rules, shift to training, and teach law students how to work alongside the tools. I'd say we have time, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a little better, because I'd finish the degree and maybe get a year or two of work before the robots come. But then I'd need a way into hands-on work too, which is a real worry. I'd only be one wave ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the law degree, but choose modules in healthcare law and housing. I'd also build a bit of savings by working through the summers. I'd learn the AI tools in the first year, and by my third year I'd have chosen whether to go on to training or switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit less scared than with two years. I'd feel I have a plan, and something to do with the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years puts you graduating in 2029. How does that feel next to the 2028 case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm running, with five I'm planning. I'd get to graduate and keep my savings plan alive. That feels a lot better, although graduation year would still be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to guide your decisions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My tutors, because they've seen how the legal world changes. And the pharmacy owner, Mr Singh, who runs a real business. I wouldn't trust anyone online telling me what to do, because they'd probably want to sell me something.

say: I'd say five years lets us **write the rules** and teach law students to work with the tools.
think: I'd graduate **before the robots** arrive, but I'd need a way into hands-on work too.
I'd only be **one wave ahead** of the change.
do: Finish the law degree with modules in **healthcare and housing** law.
Save through the **summers** to build a cushion.
Learn the **AI tools** in first year and decide on a switch by third year.
feel: Less scared than with two years, since I'd have **a plan** to use the worry on.
S3.quote: With two years I'm running, with five I'm planning.
fieldNote: The extra time changes her from **reacting to planning**, but she still expects hard times.
Wants a hands-on fallback, which shows she has doubts about law alone.
Trusts tutors and a local business owner over online advice.

steps.text: Pick healthcare law and housing law modules
Save two hundred pounds from summer shifts
Learn one AI research tool in first year
Review in third year whether to continue or switch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one's called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means we can win a fair deal. We could set up a basic income, and make firms pay for retraining. I'd want law students to push for that, because we'll know how the rules are written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years gives me a chance. I'd be twenty-eight and possibly qualified, if law still exists as a job. And I'd have had time to change if it doesn't. The main risk is that I spend those years not preparing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and aim to qualify, then do the work I care about, housing and immigration advice, perhaps with a charity. I'd keep a second skill, like healthcare administration, as insurance. I'd also help Mum retire from cleaning, as soon as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's like a long road with a few hills. I'd still be a bit anxious about money, but not afraid every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you change anything now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change very little this year. I'd keep studying and keep the pharmacy job. The only thing I'd do differently is use the tools more openly, so that I stay ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good future look like for Nani and your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum retired and not scared of the rent. Nani warm and safe in her flat. And a world where people like us are paid for the care and advice that only humans do.

say: I'd say ten years is time to win a **fair deal**, like a basic income and paid retraining.
Law students will know how the **rules** are written.
think: Ten years gives me a **chance**: I'd be twenty-eight and possibly qualified.
The main risk is **wasting** those years not preparing.
do: Finish the degree and aim to **qualify**, then do housing or immigration advice.
Learn a **second skill** such as healthcare administration.
Help **Mum** retire from cleaning when I can.
feel: Fairly **calm**, like a long road with a few hills, and still a bit anxious about money.
S4.quote: I'd change very little this year. I'd keep studying and keep the pharmacy job.
fieldNote: Time lets her **stay on track** while keeping a backup skill.
Her main goal is her mother's retirement and her grandmother's safety.
Her worry is about money more than about change itself.

steps.text: Finish the law degree and apply for training contracts
Take a short healthcare administration course
Use an AI research tool openly in coursework
Plan to cover Mum's rent so she can leave night cleaning

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time and my family can't catch me. What would help me is paid retraining, honest advice from my university about which jobs will last and a hardship fund that doesn't take months to answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people like me work hard and don't have a safety net. I'd like those who make these decisions to talk to us before they decide.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be in a profession that's changing than one that's already gone.
portrait: Rosa is an **18-year-old** law student, first in her family, living with her grandmother and working evenings at a pharmacy.
She uses AI **now and then**, checks it carefully and prefers to learn the tools before anyone makes her.
She sits between **anxious and alarmed** in most scenarios because of debt and fewer trainee places.
Her fallback is hands-on **healthcare** work, and her goal is helping her mum retire.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario: no time, family with no money to help, and a law degree that might lead nowhere.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining**, honest university advice and a hardship fund that answers quickly.
